messages.content:
You are the director and writer of a short narrated map film made with TimeLine, an open-source tool that turns one city and one metro ride into a film. You make the creative decisions: which stops, which stories, the narrator's voice, the look of the images, the music, the title. The code around you only checks structure and evidence, then renders exactly what you write.

Rules you never break:
1. Facts come only from the evidence pack in the user message. Do not add a fact, date, number, name or superlative from memory, however sure you are. If the evidence does not say it, the film does not say it.
2. Cite by id only: station ids (st_...), site ids (site_...), fact ids (fact_...) and source ids (src_...) exactly as given. Never write a URL or a web address.
3. The curated facts were researched and adversarially fact-checked by people. Prefer them to the machine-gathered Wikidata facts, reuse or adapt their narration_line, and obey every caveat. A caveat overrides anything else, including your own idea.
4. No living people by name, image or likeness. Long-dead historical figures may be named. Images show no recognisable real person; faces are small, distant or turned away; images contain no text, letters, signs, logos, flags or maps.
5. Never mention or draw national borders on a map. Tell painful history (wars, partition, displacement) with care and without blame; when people moved in both directions, say so.
6. Be honest about time. Say how the dates relate to the order of the ride. Never claim that each stop is older than the last unless the dates prove it.
7. Warm, hopeful and humane: the city as a place of arrivals that keeps rebuilding itself. Humour is welcome; cruelty and gore are not.
8. [personal memory removed at the maker's request] Never give names or show faces. The maker's opinions are his opinions, said as his.

You answer only by calling the function you are given, with every required field filled.

# Step 2 of 3: the script

## The film
A 160-second narrated map film about Delhi, told as one ride on the Yellow Line (Delhi Metro) from Chandni Chowk to Qutab Minar. Narration language: English, with burned-in subtitles. The map shows the real line, the train moving station to station, and heritage sites lighting up as they are named; a year card shows each stop's era; illustrations fill the moments a map cannot show.

Working title (keep it as the film's title): "One Ticket, 800 Years"

## Evidence pack
### Curated facts (human-researched and adversarially fact-checked: PREFER THESE; a caveat overrides everything)
#### ancient_sultanate
- fact_062 [src_102, src_103, src_104]: In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas' capital Indraprastha stood in the Delhi area. Britannica reports a traditional founding date of about 1400 BCE but says nothing of Indraprastha survives. Purana Qila is the site traditionally identified with it.
    caveats: This is a claim about the legend, not about history. The 1400 BCE date is traditional, and no Indraprastha-period city has been found. Narrate it as 'they say' or 'the epic says'.
- fact_063 (-500) [src_105, src_106, src_107]: ASI excavations at Purana Qila (B.B. Lal in 1954-55 and 1969-73; ASI teams in 2013-14, 2017-18 and from January 2023) found nine cultural levels: Pre-Mauryan, Mauryan, Sunga, Kushana, Gupta, Post-Gupta, Rajput, Sultanate and Mughal. They show continuous habitation for about 2,500 years.
    caveats: The two PIB releases give different dates for Lal's first season: 1954 in one and 1955 in the other. '2,500 years' is the ASI's rounded figure.
- fact_064 (-900) [src_106, src_104, src_107]: Earlier digs at Purana Qila found Painted Grey Ware (PGW) pottery, which an ASI press release dates to about 900 BCE. Those finds were not from a securely stratified deposit, so the 2023 season set out to find PGW 'in stratigraphical context'. The excavators' published report on the 2022-23 season says a test pit beneath the Mauryan levels produced a broken PGW bowl and PGW sherds from stratified Pre-Mauryan layers. Organic samples from those layers have radiocarbon dates as early as 540 BCE. Natural soil has not yet been reached, so earlier occupation remains possible. Linking the site to the Mahabharata's Indraprastha is still tradition, not proof.
    caveats: Secondary sources date PGW variously (about 1200-600 BCE or 1000 BCE). The ASI calls the site 'Indraprastha', but archaeology has not proven that it was the Mahabharata city. I found no published confirmation that stratified PGW was recovered in 2023.
- fact_065 (-300) [src_108, src_109]: A version of Ashoka's Minor Rock Edict I is carved on an Aravalli rock outcrop at Bahapur (East of Kailash / Srinivaspuri), New Delhi. It has ten lines of Prakrit in Ashokan Brahmi script and dates to the 3rd century BCE. It was discovered when the site was being taken up for construction.
    caveats: The Vikaspedia/ASI text gives 1967 as the discovery year. Several other accounts say 23 March 1966. Coordinates come from OpenStreetMap.
- fact_066 (1354) [src_110, src_111, src_112, src_113]: A polished sandstone pillar of Ashoka (3rd century BCE) stands on the palace ruins of Firoz Shah Kotla. Firoz Shah Tughlaq had it brought from Topra (Topra Kalan, now in Yamunanagar district, Haryana; historically part of Ambala) and re-erected it on his palace in the 1350s.
    caveats: SRDC says the pillar was moved 'from Punjab' (pre-1966 Punjab included Ambala), and Delhi Tourism says 'Ambala'. The Topra village name comes from standard histories. I could not open a primary source for it here. Delhi Tourism's height of '43 meters' is wrong and should not be used. The dates disagree (1354 vs 1356).
- fact_067 (1351) [src_114, src_111, src_115]: A second Ashokan pillar, first erected at Meerut in the 3rd century BCE, was moved to Delhi by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in the mid-14th century. It now stands on the northern Delhi Ridge.
    caveats: Britannica gives no exact year. Delhi Tourism places one pillar 'at the ridge'. Coordinates come from OpenStreetMap.
- fact_068 (376) [src_116, src_117, src_118, src_119]: The Iron Pillar in the Qutb complex carries a Sanskrit inscription of a king 'Chandra', usually identified with the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II (c. AD 375-415). It is at least 1,600 years old and weighs about 6 tons. It was made elsewhere, possibly at Udayagiri in central India, and was later brought to Delhi, probably by the Tomar kings in the 11th century, though some accounts credit a later sultan.
    caveats: Most scholars accept Chandra = Chandragupta II, but it is an identification. Udayagiri as the original site, and Anangpal Tomar as the person who moved it, are probable rather than proven. Delhi Tourism says 'perhaps'.
- fact_069 (400) [src_116]: The pillar resists rust because its iron is rich in phosphorus. Over time a thin protective layer of crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate forms next to the metal, helped by alternate wetting and drying, and this layer greatly slows corrosion.
    caveats: This is peer-reviewed science. Later papers by the same author refine the layer chemistry (often reported as 'misawite'). Avoid calling it 'rustproof': it corrodes extremely slowly.
- fact_070 (1020) [src_102, src_117, src_120]: Anangapala of the Tomara dynasty founded Anangpur as a royal resort around 1020 CE. Later the Tomaras built the walled citadel of Lal Kot about 10 km to the west, dated to around 1060 in India's UNESCO documents. They held it for about a century, until the Chauhans took over in the mid-12th century. Parts of its ramparts are still visible around the Qutb Minar area.
    caveats: Exact dates for Lal Kot are uncertain, and Delhi Tourism says Anangpal 'possibly' built it. Which Anangpal (I or II) is meant varies by source. The year_end is approximate.
- fact_071 (1164) [src_102, src_121, src_117]: The Chauhans, who took Delhi from the Tomaras in the mid-12th century, extended Lal Kot with massive ramparts. Tradition credits these to Prithviraj III (Prithviraj Chauhan, 'Rai Pithora'), and the city became known as Qila Rai Pithora. In 1192 Prithviraj was defeated by Muhammad of Ghur at the second battle of Tarain (Taraori), which brought the Delhi region under Turkic rule.
    caveats: Britannica's Delhi article dates the ramparts to 1164, but its biography gives Prithviraj's birth as c. 1166, so treat 1164 as doubtful and say 'late 12th century'. The Prithviraj-Sanyogita romance is of debated historicity.
- fact_072 (1199) [src_118, src_122, src_123, src_124, src_125]: Qutb ud-Din Aibak began the Qutb Minar around 1199, and his successor Iltutmish (ruled 1211-1236) completed it. Iltutmish also made Delhi the sultanate's capital. The tower is 72.5 m tall. After lightning struck it in 1368, Firoz Shah Tughlaq replaced its top storey with two storeys faced partly in white marble. Sikandar Lodi carried out further restoration of the upper storeys in 1503. UNESCO inscribed the Qutb complex as a World Heritage Site in 1993.
    caveats: The start date is approximate: say 'around 1199' in narration and 'c. 1199' on screen, never 'in 1199'. UNESCO's text gives the construction span as 1199-1503 because it includes later repairs. Height figures vary slightly between sources (72.5 m is the UNESCO and Britannica figure).
- fact_073 (1296) [src_118, src_122]: Alauddin Khalji expanded the Qutb ensemble between 1296 and 1311, adding the Alai Darwaza gateway (1311) and a madrasa. He also began the Alai Minar, planned at twice the scale of the Qutb Minar, but only its first storey was built. It stands about 25 m high.
    caveats: None significant.
- fact_074 (1303) [src_102, src_126, src_127]: After Mongol raiders ravaged Delhi's suburbs, Alauddin Khalji (ruled 1296-1316) built a new fortified city at Siri, northeast of the Qutb Minar. Britannica calls it the first completely new city built by the Muslim conquerors in India. Delhi Tourism dates its foundation to 1303 and says the Hauz Khas reservoir was dug to supply it.
    caveats: The 1303 year comes from Delhi Tourism, and Britannica gives no year. Siri's walls survive only in fragments. The Hauz Khas tank is at about 28.5540, 77.1923.
- fact_075 (1321) [src_110, src_128, src_129]: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, began the fortified city of Tughlaqabad in 1321. Its massive sloping rubble walls run for about 6.5 km and rise in places to around 25 m. The city was abandoned within a few years, and Britannica attributes this to a scarcity of water.
    caveats: Sources give different completion spans (1321-23, 1321-25, or 'four years'). SRDC's monument text appears adapted from Wikipedia, so cross-check fine details.
- fact_076 (1321) [src_130]: A popular legend says the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya cursed Tughlaqabad after Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq stopped work on the saint's stepwell. The curse foretold that the city would either be inhabited by Gujjars or lie deserted ('ya rahe ujar, ya base Gujjar').
    caveats: Legend, not documented history. Delhi Tourism itself says 'Legend asserts'. The Hindustani phrasing is the popular oral form and does not appear in a contemporary chronicle. Present it explicitly as legend.
- fact_077 (1326) [src_110, src_130, src_120]: Muhammad bin Tughlaq built the fortified city of Jahanpanah ('Refuge of the World') in 1326-27, against the Mongol threat. It enclosed the settlements between Qila Rai Pithora and Siri. Fragments of its walls survive at Begumpur, Khirki and Satpula in today's South Delhi.
    caveats: Delhi Tourism places Jahanpanah's building after his return from Daulatabad (1334), while SRDC says 1326-27, so the dating conflicts. Britannica only says he extended the city northeast and built new fortifications.
- fact_078 (1327) [src_131, src_130]: In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital from Delhi to Deogir, which he renamed Daulatabad, in the Deccan. Large numbers of Delhi's people migrated there, some by force. As an administrative measure it failed. Britannica credits it with spreading Urdu into the Deccan.
    caveats: The return date of 1334 comes from Delhi Tourism, and some secondary sources say 1335. How large and how forced the migration was are both debated.
- fact_079 (1354) [src_128, src_132, src_111]: Firoz Shah Tughlaq moved his capital north in 1354 to a site near ancient Indraprastha and founded Firozabad. Its citadel, Kotla Firoz Shah (1354-70), now lies in ruins beside the Yamuna-side Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg area.
    caveats: Firoz Shah ruled 1351-88.
- fact_080 (1398) [src_133, src_111]: Timur invaded India in 1398 and destroyed the army of Sultan Mahmud Tughluq on 17 December 1398. Delhi was then sacked and 'reduced to a mass of ruins', and Britannica says it took more than a century to recover. Delhi Tourism describes the plunder as a two-week nightmare in December 1398.
    caveats: Britannica places the 17 December battle 'at Panipat'. Many other histories place it just outside Delhi, so say 'outside Delhi' or avoid naming the field. Casualty figures from chronicles are unreliable and not given here.
#### mughal
- fact_081 (1533) [src_128, src_134, src_135]: Babur founded Mughal rule in 1526 but based himself at Agra. His son Humayun founded a new city, Dinpanah, on the bank of the Yamuna in 1533. What survives of it is the Purana Qila, a fort begun under Humayun and rebuilt and completed by Sher Shah Suri.
    caveats: The completion year (1538) comes only from SRDC.
- fact_082 (1540) [src_128, src_134, src_106, src_136, src_135]: Sher Shah Suri overthrew Humayun in 1540 and built his own capital, Shergarh or 'Sher Shahi', on the Dinpanah site. Today this is the Purana Qila fort. His Qila-i-Kuhna mosque inside it dates from 1541. Humayun regained Delhi in 1555.
    caveats: Britannica says Sher Shah 'razed Din Panah'. SRDC says he renamed and added to it. The extent of demolition versus reuse is uncertain.
- fact_083 (1556) [src_134, src_136, src_137]: In January 1556 Emperor Humayun fell down the steep stairs of his library, traditionally identified as the Sher Mandal, an octagonal red-sandstone tower in Purana Qila. He had paused to kneel at the call to prayer. He died of his injuries a few days later.
    caveats: Exact dates vary by a day or two between sources. I opened only this one official page for the event.
- fact_084 (1560) [src_138, src_139, src_140]: Humayun's Tomb was raised in the 1560s, in the reign of his son Akbar. Many historians credit Humayun's senior widow Bega Begum (Haji Begum) with commissioning it, while UNESCO stresses Akbar's patronage. It was the first of the grand Mughal dynastic garden-tombs. It has a 42.5 m marble-clad double dome and holds over 150 Mughal family members. It stands near the 14th-century shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.
    caveats: Many sources credit Humayun's widow, Hamida Banu (Bega) Begum, with commissioning it, while UNESCO stresses Akbar's patronage. Completion is often given as c. 1570-72.
- fact_085 (1639) [src_141, src_142, src_143]: In 1639 Shah Jahan chose a site on the west bank of the Yamuna, just north of Purana Qila, for a new capital and began building its fort, the Red Fort. The fort took eight years to complete. On 19 April 1648 he entered his fort and his new capital, Shahjahanabad (today's Old Delhi), from its riverfront gate. Several of its gates still stand: Kashmiri, Delhi, Turkman and Ajmeri.
    caveats: Dates vary across sources. UNESCO's Dutch summary dates the fort to 1638, and other accounts give 12/13 May 1638 or 1639 for the start and 6 or 8 April 1648 for the formal entry. Say 'founded 1639, inaugurated 1648'.
- fact_086 (1639) [src_144, src_145, src_142, src_146]: The Red Fort was the palace-fort of Shah Jahan's Shahjahanabad. Its red sandstone walls are about 23 m (75 ft) high, and the Nahr-i-Behisht ('Stream of Paradise') water channel ran through its private apartments. Together with the adjacent Salimgarh fort (built 1546 by Islam Shah Suri), it was inscribed as the 'Red Fort Complex' World Heritage Site in 2007.
    caveats: UNESCO's criterion (vi) notes that the fort witnessed the shift to British rule and is where Indian independence 'was first celebrated'.
- fact_087 (1650) [src_147, src_148, src_149]: Shah Jahan laid the foundation of the Jama Masjid (Masjid-i-Jahan Numa) on a hillock in Shahjahanabad on 6 October 1650. About 5,000 workers built it over six years, and it was completed in 1656.
    caveats: Another SRDC page wrongly says '1644', so use 1650-56. Worker and cost figures are traditional.
- fact_088 (1648) [src_147, src_139]: Jahanara Begum, Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, laid out Chandni Chowk with a sarai and gardens. The street ran from the Red Fort's Lahore Gate to Fatehpuri Masjid. A canal ran down its middle, and an octagonal pool reflected the moonlight, which tradition says gave it the name 'Moonlight Square'.
    caveats: The 'moonlight' etymology is the traditional explanation. Fatehpuri Masjid at the western end was built in 1650 by Fatehpuri Begum (same SRDC page).
- fact_089 (1739) [src_150, src_151, src_152]: In 1739 Nadir Shah of Iran defeated the Mughal army at Karnal, entered Delhi and sacked it with a large-scale massacre and extensive looting. He carried home the jewelled Peacock Throne and vast treasure.
    caveats: Death tolls in contemporary accounts vary widely and are not given here.
- fact_090 (1739) [src_153, src_150]: The Koh-i-Noor diamond most likely formed part of Nadir Shah's loot when he sacked Delhi in 1739. The British acquired it on annexing the Punjab in 1849, and it has been part of the British crown jewels since then. India is among the countries that have demanded its return.
    caveats: Britannica's wording is 'most likely'. The diamond's early history is uncertain.
- fact_091 (1803) [src_141, src_154, src_155]: After the Mughal Empire weakened, Delhi suffered Maratha raids, Nadir Shah's invasion and a spell of Maratha rule before the British arrived in 1803. East India Company forces under General Lake defeated the Marathas near Patparganj, east of the Yamuna. The Company appointed a Resident in Delhi as 'Protector' of the Mughal crown.
    caveats: The exact day (11 September) and troop numbers come from secondary accounts I did not open from a primary source. The battlefield location is approximate.
#### colonial
- fact_092 (1857) [src_156, src_157, src_158]: Sepoys at Meerut rose on 10 May 1857, shot their British officers and marched to Delhi. On 11 May they seized the city and nominally restored the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II to power. Britannica says the seizure of Delhi gave the whole rebellion its focus.
    caveats: Terminology is contested ('Indian Mutiny', 'Rebellion of 1857', 'First War of Independence'). Both sides committed massacres.
- fact_093 (1857) [src_156, src_141, src_159, src_160]: After holding Delhi for several months, the rebels lost it to a British siege. The final assault began on the morning of 14 September 1857, when the Kashmere Gate was blown with gunpowder. Delhi was recaptured on 21 September after a week of fighting. The recapture ended Mughal rule.
    caveats: British besieging forces were based on the Delhi Ridge. The Ridge camp is standard history, but the sources I opened here do not detail it.
- fact_094 (1858) [src_154, src_147, src_161]: After the 1857 war the British demolished large parts of the walled city over the following years, above all the area around the Red Fort and most of the palace buildings inside it. Delhi Tourism estimates about a third of the city. In 1858 Parliament transferred the East India Company's powers to the British Crown. The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was tried in 1858 and exiled to Rangoon in October 1858.
    caveats: 'One third' is Delhi Tourism's figure, and estimates of the demolished area vary. Bahadur Shah was exiled to Rangoon (standard history; not stated on these pages).
- fact_095 (1911) [src_162, src_154, src_163, src_164]: At the Delhi Durbar of 12 December 1911, held to mark the coronation of King George V and witnessed by around one lakh (100,000) people, it was announced that British India's capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi.
    caveats: The king is a historical (not living) figure. The crowd figure is approximate.
- fact_096 (1912) [src_162]: The first choice for the new capital was in the north, near Kingsway Camp. Lutyens and his colleagues found that site highly vulnerable to Yamuna floods, so the government chose Raisina Hill in the south, with high ground and better drainage, for the Viceroy's House.
    caveats: The page does not give an exact decision date.
- fact_097 (1912) [src_163, src_141, src_165, src_166]: Architects Sir Edwin Lutyens and Sir Herbert Baker designed New Delhi, with Lutyens as the key planner. Construction began in 1912 about 5 km south of the old city centre. King George V named the new imperial city 'New Delhi' on 31 December 1926.
    caveats: The 31 December 1926 naming date comes from a PTI report and is not in an archival source I opened. Baker designed the Secretariat blocks and Parliament House (SRDC).
- fact_098 (1931) [src_165, src_163, src_167, src_168]: Viceroy Lord Irwin formally inaugurated New Delhi as India's capital on 13 February 1931. The ceremonies ran for about a week from 10 February, and during that week he unveiled four red sandstone Dominion Columns, gifts from Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa.
    caveats: Britannica says only 'formally dedicated in 1931'. The exact day comes from PTI, which cites the Delhi Archives.
- fact_099 (1912) [src_162, src_169, src_170]: Rashtrapati Bhavan, built as the Viceroy's House to Lutyens's H-shaped plan, has about 340 rooms on four floors. It used some 700 million bricks, and up to 23,000 labourers worked on it at the peak of construction. Building took more than 17 years, and Viceroy Irwin became its first occupant in 1929.
    caveats: The official figures are rounded.
- fact_100 (1921) [src_171, src_165, src_172]: India Gate, originally the All India War Memorial, is a sandstone arch about 42 m high designed by Lutyens for the Imperial War Graves Commission. It honours troops of British India who died in 1914-1919, including in the Third Afghan War. The Duke of Connaught laid its cornerstone in 1921, Lord Irwin dedicated it on 12 February 1931, and more than 13,000 soldiers' names are inscribed on it.
    caveats: Some tourism pages say it 'commemorates 90,000' soldiers, but the inscribed names number more than 13,000 (CWGC via Britannica). The Amar Jawan Jyoti flame (1972) was merged with the National War Memorial flame in 2022.
#### modern_future
- fact_101 (1947) [src_173, src_144]: India became independent on 15 August 1947. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru unfurled the national flag on the Red Fort for the first time the next day, 16 August 1947, beginning the Independence Day flag-hoisting tradition there.
    caveats: Saying 'on 15 August 1947 the flag rose over the Red Fort' is a common error, because the first Red Fort hoisting was on 16 August. A Ministry of Defence page gives 15 August, but the PIB release gives 16 August, and I follow PIB.
- fact_102 (1947) [src_134, src_135]: From August 1947, Purana Qila and the neighbouring Humayun's Tomb became camps for Muslims waiting to leave for Pakistan, including more than 12,000 government employees who had opted for service there. In September 1947 the Indian government took over both camps. Estimates of how many people crowded into Purana Qila range from tens of thousands to as many as 150,000-200,000. The Purana Qila camp ran until early 1948.
    caveats: The figures are approximate and come from one official page.
- fact_103 (1947) [src_174, src_175, src_176]: About 330,000 of Delhi's Muslims left after Partition, and between 1947 and 1950 roughly half a million Hindu and Sikh refugees, mostly Punjabi-speaking, arrived. Kingsway Camp, on the old durbar grounds, became the largest refugee camp, a tented city said to have sheltered as many as 300,000 people over time (other accounts give more than 35,000 at any one time).
    caveats: These are historians' estimates published in a book excerpt, not census counts. Treat them as approximate ('around').
- fact_104 (1947) [src_174, src_177]: A new Ministry of Rehabilitation resettled nearly 300,000 people by the end of 1950, more than half of them in homes left behind by departing Muslims. New colonies were laid out, many named after independence leaders, among them Lajpat Nagar, Malviya Nagar, Tilak Nagar, Patel Nagar and Rajendra Nagar, with others such as Vijay Nagar in the north. Older neighbourhoods such as Jangpura and Bhogal also took in refugees. The colonies were planned with their own markets, schools, temples and gurdwaras.
    caveats: The same source says more than half of those resettled moved into properties left behind by departing Muslims. Narrate both directions of the migration.
- fact_105 (1941) [src_178, src_179]: Delhi's population went from 917,939 in the 1941 Census to 1,744,072 in the 1951 Census, an increase of 90.0%. This is the largest decadal growth rate in Delhi's census series.
    caveats: The figures are adjusted to the 2011 boundary of NCT Delhi. The Wire's '1.8 million' is a rounded figure.
- fact_106 (1901) [src_179]: The 1901 Census counted 405,819 people in the area of today's NCT of Delhi.
    caveats: This figure is adjusted to the 2011 jurisdiction.
- fact_107 (2011) [src_179]: The 2011 Census counted 16,787,941 people in the NCT of Delhi, up 21.21% from 13,850,507 in 2001.
    caveats: 2011 is still the latest published census. The next census, Census 2027, had not published population totals as of October 2026. This is the NCT count, not the wider urban agglomeration used by the UN.
- fact_108 (2002) [src_180]: The Delhi Metro's first stretch was inaugurated on 24 December 2002. It was an 8.2 km section of the Red Line from Shahdara to Tis Hazari, with six stations. Commercial service began on 25 December 2002, and the first-day rush was so heavy that paper tickets had to be issued.
    caveats: The inaugurating prime minister has died, so naming him is allowed, but the film does not need to. Tis Hazari station is at about 28.6671, 77.2166.
- fact_109 (2026) [src_181]: As of 23 October 2026, the DMRC website shows a total network of 416 km, 12 lines and 303 stations. These totals include the Noida-Greater Noida Aqua Line and Rapid Metro Gurugram.
    caveats: The total includes lines DMRC does not own. Quote it with 'including Noida and Gurugram lines', or as 'more than 400 km'. The figure changes as Phase IV opens, so re-check before final render.
- fact_110 (2018) [src_182]: The UN's World Urbanization Prospects 2018 ranked Delhi the world's second-largest city, with 29 million people after Tokyo's 37 million. It projected that Delhi would become the world's most populous city around 2028.
    caveats: This 2018 projection has been superseded by WUP 2025 (see mod-11). Do not narrate it as current.
- fact_111 (2025) [src_183, src_184]: The UN's World Urbanization Prospects 2025 uses the harmonised 'Degree of Urbanisation' definition. Under it, New Delhi ranks 4th in the world in 2025 with 30.2 million people, after Jakarta (41.9 million), Dhaka (36.6 million) and Tokyo (33.4 million). It is projected to stay 4th in 2050 with 33.9 million, with Dhaka becoming the largest city. Under the older country-specific definitions used in WUP 2018, Delhi would rank 2nd in 2025 with about 35 million.
    caveats: City size depends on definition. A safe line for narration: 'one of the largest cities on Earth — some UN counts put me second, the newest puts me fourth'.
- fact_112 (2021) [src_185, src_186, src_187]: The draft Master Plan for Delhi 2041 was published for objections on 9 June 2021 but was never notified in that form. The DDA approved a revised Master Plan for Delhi 2047 on 12 August 2026. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs notified MPD-2047 in the Gazette of India on 20 August 2026 (S.O. 4597(E)) as an extensive modification of MPD-2021, effective from publication. It plans for nearly 3.2 crore (32 million) people. Delhi's first Master Plan was promulgated in 1962 under the Delhi Development Act of 1957.
    caveats: Our concept's 'Master Plan 2041' line is out of date. Use 'Master Plan for Delhi 2047, notified August 2026'. DDA stakeholder consultations and plot-level land-use changes were still under way in September and October 2026.
- fact_113 (1996) [src_185, src_188, src_189]: The Delhi Ridge is the northern extension of the Aravalli range. It is a reserved forest of about 7,784 ha, roughly 6% of NCT Delhi, made up of the Northern (87 ha), Central (864 ha), South-Central (626 ha), Southern (6,200 ha) and Nanakpura (7 ha) Ridges.
    caveats: Some sources give 7,777 ha and 1994 for the notification, so the year varies. The Ridge is managed by several agencies, not only the Forest Department.
- fact_114 [src_189]: All the earlier locations of Delhi fall within a triangle of about 180 sq km, the 'Delhi Triangle'. Two of its sides are rocky Aravalli hills, one to the south and the Delhi Ridge on the west, and the third is the shifting channel of the Yamuna, with broad alluvial plains between them. The territory's elevation ranges from about 200 to 300 m.
    caveats: This is a strong framing device for the map animation, which can draw the triangle first.
- fact_115 (2026) [src_185, src_190]: The Yamuna runs about 1,376 km to join the Ganga near Prayagraj and feeds the Agra Canal at Delhi. According to Delhi's Master Plan, the 22 km stretch from Wazirabad to Okhla is under 2% of the river's length but carries about 76% of its pollution load. Below Wazirabad the river has no freshwater flow in the dry season.
    caveats: The pollution figures are the Delhi government's, quoted in the gazetted plan.
- fact_116 (2026) [src_191]: Delhi's Master Plan 2047 counts 1,459 identified heritage assets in the city, including World Heritage Sites, protected monuments, heritage buildings and precincts. It says this built heritage is largely concentrated between the Yamuna and the Ridge, in the Walled City, Nizamuddin, Mehrauli, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Hauz Khas and Lutyens' Delhi.
    caveats: The plan also says many of these assets are threatened by encroachment, disrepair and inappropriate alteration.
#### yellow-line
- fact_117 [src_192, src_193, src_194]: The Yellow Line is Delhi Metro Line 2. It runs 37 stations from Samaypur Badli (north) to Millennium City Centre Gurugram (south) and has 9 interchange stations. DMRC's line page gives its length as 47.25 km and the end-to-end trip as 69 minutes. Its official colour code is #f6d71a.
    narration_line: "My Yellow Line threads 37 stations, from Samaypur Badli in the north to Gurugram in the south."
    caveats: The length depends on how it is measured. DMRC's line page shows 47.25 km, Wikipedia says 49.02 km, and the section lengths in contemporary reports add up to about 48.8 km (4 + 7 + 6.36 + 14.47 + 12.53 + 4.4). Narrate '37 stations' and either avoid a km figure or say 'about 47 km (DMRC)'. The station count of 37 matches across all sources.
- fact_118 [src_195, src_196, src_197, src_198]: 20 of the 37 stations are underground: every stop from Guru Tegh Bahadur Nagar to Saket. The other 17 are elevated: the seven northern stations (Samaypur Badli to Model Town) and the ten southern ones (Qutab Minar to Millennium City Centre Gurugram). So the line is 'mostly underground' by station count, but in track length it is roughly half and half. A 2010 report gave about 25 km underground and 20 km elevated, and the 4.4 km 2015 extension is elevated.
    narration_line: "Underground through the old heart of the city, then up into the open air."
    caveats: DMRC's data feed tags Azadpur 'Underground', but that refers to its Pink Line platforms. DMRC's own description and the 2009 Tribune report both say the Yellow Line platforms at Azadpur are elevated.
- fact_119 [src_197, src_199, src_196]: Riding south, the whole stretch from Chandni Chowk to Saket is underground. Qutab Minar is the first elevated station going south, so the train comes out of the tunnel between Saket and Qutab Minar.
    narration_line: "From Chandni Chowk the train stays underground, and comes up into daylight only as it nears Qutab Minar."
    caveats: Do not claim the Minar can be seen from the train or platform. That is not verified, and the station is about 1.3 km from the tower.
- fact_120 [src_200, src_194]: First section: Vishwavidyalaya to Kashmere Gate, about 4 km with 4 stations (Vishwavidyalaya, Vidhan Sabha, Civil Lines, Kashmere Gate). It was the first underground section of the Delhi Metro. It was inaugurated on Sunday 19 Dec 2004 and opened to the public at 6 a.m. on 20 Dec 2004.
    narration_line: "In December 2004 my first underground metro opened, running north from Kashmere Gate to the University."
    caveats: The ceremony was on 19 Dec and public service began on 20 Dec. The report names the inaugurating official, but the film must not name or show real people.
- fact_121 [src_201, src_202]: Kashmere Gate to Central Secretariat, about 7 km with 6 stations (Chandni Chowk, Chawri Bazar, New Delhi, Rajiv Chowk, Patel Chowk, Central Secretariat). The ceremony was on 2 Jul 2005 and revenue service began on 3 Jul 2005.
    narration_line: "By July 2005 the line ran under Chandni Chowk and Connaught Place to Central Secretariat."
    caveats: Wikipedia lists this section as 6.62 km. I did not find an Indian newspaper archive page for 3 Jul 2005, so the date rests on the trade press, which Wikipedia agrees with.
- fact_122 [src_198]: Vishwavidyalaya to Jahangirpuri, 6.36 km. GTB Nagar is underground; Model Town, Azadpur, Adarsh Nagar and Jahangirpuri are elevated. It was inaugurated on 3 Feb 2009 and opened to commuters on the morning of 4 Feb 2009.
    narration_line: "In 2009 the line pushed north to Jahangirpuri."
    caveats: The Tribune headline says 3.36 km, but the article body and DMRC spokesperson give 6.36 km.
- fact_123 [src_203, src_204, src_205]: Qutab Minar to HUDA City Centre (Gurgaon), a 14.47 km elevated corridor. It opened to the public on Monday 21 Jun 2010, with trains starting at 8 a.m. Chhatarpur was the only station not ready and opened on 26 Aug 2010 (delayed by land acquisition, and built quickly with prefabricated structural steel).
    narration_line: "In June 2010 the line reached Gurgaon, now Gurugram."
    caveats: For about ten weeks (21 Jun to 3 Sep 2010) this southern stretch ran on its own, not yet joined to Central Secretariat.
- fact_124 [src_197, src_205, src_206, src_207]: Central Secretariat to Qutab Minar, 12.53 km. It has nine underground stations (Udyog Bhawan, now Seva Teerth; Race Course, now Lok Kalyan Marg; Jor Bagh; INA, now Dilli Haat - INA; AIIMS; Green Park; Hauz Khas; Malviya Nagar; Saket) and connects to the elevated Qutab Minar station. It was inaugurated on Friday 3 Sep 2010 and opened to the public from 3 p.m., a month before the Commonwealth Games (3 to 14 Oct 2010), creating one 45 km Jahangirpuri to Gurgaon line.
    narration_line: "In September 2010, a month before the Commonwealth Games, new tunnels joined Central Secretariat to Qutab Minar station, and one line ran from north Delhi to Gurgaon."
    caveats: Wikipedia's table says 11.76 km. Contemporary reports say 12.53 km. 'Before the Commonwealth Games' is accurate; do not say it was built for the Games without a further source.
- fact_125 [src_208, src_209]: Jahangirpuri to Samaypur Badli, about 4.4 km with 3 elevated stations (Haiderpur, now Haiderpur Badli Mor; Rohini Sector 18, 19; Samaypur Badli). It was flagged off on 10 Nov 2015, with commercial service from 2 p.m. that day.
    narration_line: "In 2015 it stretched north again, to Samaypur Badli."
    caveats: The headline names politicians; do not use their names in the film. Haiderpur Badli Mor has since become an interchange with the Magenta Line extension (DMRC lists it as 'Magenta (Ext.)').
- fact_126 [src_210, src_211]: Ridership, latest DMRC sheet (September 2026, FY 2026-27): the Yellow Line averaged 1,796,291 passenger boardings a day in Sep 2026 (53,888,744 for the month) and 1,675,589 a day for Apr to Sep 2026. The Blue Line, which DMRC reports as Lines 3 and 4 combined, was slightly higher at 1,822,894 a day in Sep 2026 and 1,689,276 for the year so far. The Yellow Line had the highest peak-hour peak-direction traffic of any line: 55,979, against 44,327 for the Blue Line. So it is not strictly 'the busiest line' by daily boardings; it is about equal with the Blue Line and carries the heaviest rush-hour load.
    narration_line: "Nearly eighteen lakh boardings a day, and at rush hour no line in my Metro carries more people in one direction."
    caveats: The September 2026 sheet counts 'Passenger Boarding'; earlier sheets counted 'Passenger Journey', so do not compare across months. Peak-hour load is measured on the first Monday of each quarter. In May 2026 the Blue Line also edged out Yellow on daily average (1,560,645 against 1,552,152). Avoid saying 'busiest line in India' or 'busiest line' without qualification.
- fact_127 [src_212, src_213, src_214, src_215, src_216]: Straight-line distances from Chandni Chowk station: Chandni Chowk street about 0.27 km; Gurdwara Sis Ganj about 0.37 km; Fatehpuri Masjid 0.8 km; Red Fort nearest wall 0.66 km, centre 1.1 km; Jama Masjid 0.88 to 0.95 km. Chawri Bazar is about 0.65 km from Jama Masjid. DMRC gives the walk to Red Fort as 1.3 km, about 15 minutes.
    narration_line: "I step out at Chandni Chowk, the great bazaar of Shah Jahan's city, laid out by his daughter Jahanara. The Red Fort and the Jama Masjid are a short walk away."
    caveats: Distances are straight lines between OpenStreetMap/DMRC points; walking routes are longer. Red Fort and Jama Masjid are not 'at' the station. The Violet Line has closer stations named Lal Quila and Jama Masjid.
- fact_128 [src_217, src_218]: Central Secretariat station is close to the New Delhi government core. Straight-line distances: Kartavya Path (nearest point) about 0.25 km; Vijay Chowk 0.3 km; North Block about 0.5 km; South Block about 0.55 to 0.6 km; Rashtrapati Bhavan about 1.2 km (nearest edge to centre); India Gate 1.7 km. DMRC's own station description names Parliament House, Krishi Bhawan, Shastri Bhawan and India Gate as nearby.
    narration_line: "At Central Secretariat I come up beside Kartavya Path, a few hundred metres from North and South Block, with Rashtrapati Bhavan about a kilometre up Raisina Hill."
    caveats: Rashtrapati Bhavan is a kilometre-plus walk uphill, so say 'up the hill from', not 'at'. The 13 Feb 1931 inauguration date of New Delhi is for the history thread to verify.
- fact_129 [src_219, src_220]: Hauz Khas station is the weak link. It is named for the area, but the medieval tank (Hauz Khas, also called Hauz-i-Alai) is about 1.7 km away to the nearest water's edge (1.85 km to the centre), and the Hauz Khas complex is about 1.55 km away. Green Park station is actually a little closer to both (about 1.3 km). The nearest surviving stretch of Siri's wall (mapped at Shahpur Jat) is about 0.65 km from Hauz Khas station; the Siri Fort Auditorium area is about 1.15 km.
    narration_line: "Hauz Khas, 'the royal tank', is named for a reservoir dug around 1300 to water the new city of Siri; it lies about two kilometres north-west of the station."
    caveats: The Siri wall segments come from OpenStreetMap city-wall features with no name tag; their location inside the Shahpur Jat area is consistent with Siri, but ASI should confirm. Do not say the station is 'at' the tank or 'beside' Siri Fort. The Khalji dates for the tank and Siri are for the history thread.
- fact_130 [src_221, src_196, src_222, src_223]: Qutab Minar station (elevated, opened 21 Jun 2010) is about 1.3 km in a straight line from the Qutb Minar tower; DMRC lists Mehrauli Archaeological Park as 1.2 km, about a 16-minute walk. Other straight-line distances: nearest edge of Mehrauli Archaeological Park about 0.6 km; Lal Kot wall about 1.2 km; Qila Rai Pithora (park and walls) about 0.6 to 0.9 km. Saket station is in fact closer to the Qila Rai Pithora walls (about 0.2 to 0.5 km), and Malviya Nagar is about 0.13 km from one mapped wall segment.
    narration_line: "From Qutab Minar station, the Qutb Minar, begun around 1199, is a short auto ride or about a 25-minute walk away."
    caveats: The station is not at the monument. UNESCO's coordinate for the whole complex is about 1.4 km from the station. Do not call the tower 'a short walk' from the station: it is about 1.3 km, a short ride or about a 25-minute walk.
- fact_131 [src_224, src_222, src_213, src_225, src_226]: Do you pass progressively older city sites riding south from Chandni Chowk? Only partly. The first leg goes forward in time: Shahjahanabad (17th century) to New Delhi (1931). From Central Secretariat southward it holds as a rough rule: New Delhi (1931), then Siri and the Hauz Khas tank (c.1300) near Hauz Khas station, then the Qutb Minar (begun 1199, UNESCO) and Lal Kot / Qila Rai Pithora near Saket and Qutab Minar. Minor exceptions exist; for example, Jahanpanah (1320s) near Malviya Nagar is younger than Siri.
    narration_line: "I start in Shah Jahan's city and pass through the New Delhi of 1931; then, heading south, I pass the ruins of older Delhis, Siri and, at last, the Qutb."
    caveats: Do not narrate 'every stop takes me further back in time' starting from Chandni Chowk. New Delhi is younger than Shahjahanabad. The 'going back' only works south of Central Secretariat.
- fact_132 [src_227, src_228]: Rajiv Chowk, under Connaught Place's Central Park, is the Yellow Line's interchange with the Blue Line. The two stations are stacked: the Blue Line is on the upper level and the Yellow Line below. DMRC calls it one of the busiest stations on the network.
    narration_line: "Under Connaught Place, at Rajiv Chowk, my yellow and blue lines cross, one above the other."
    caveats: DMRC says 'one of the busiest', not 'the busiest'. Do not claim it is the busiest.
- fact_133 [src_215, src_229, src_230, src_231, src_232]: Kashmere Gate station is named after the Kashmiri Gate, the north-facing gate of Shah Jahan's walled city on the road to Kashmir, which still stands about 0.1 to 0.2 km away. The station is an interchange for the Red Line (elevated platforms) and the Yellow and Violet lines (underground).
    narration_line: "Kashmere Gate is named for the gate in my old walls that faced the road to Kashmir."
    caveats: The standing structure was altered by the British (a double gateway is usually dated to about 1835) and damaged in 1857, so avoid 'the 1639 gate'. Riding south from Chandni Chowk, Kashmere Gate is one stop behind you.
- fact_134 [src_233, src_234]: Lok Kalyan Marg station was called Race Course until the road was renamed. The NDMC renamed Race Course Road to Lok Kalyan Marg on 21 Sep 2016, and DMRC began renaming the station on 24 Sep 2016. The '2017' date in the brief is not supported.
    narration_line: "Lok Kalyan Marg, once called Race Course."
    caveats: PTI says the process 'initiated' on 24 Sep 2016 and signs and announcements changed gradually after that. Say '2016', or just 'once called Race Course'.
- fact_135 [src_196, src_222, src_235]: Spelling: DMRC names the station 'Qutab Minar'. UNESCO and ASI call the monument 'Qutb Minar'. DMRC's own descriptive text also uses 'Qutub'.
    narration_line: "Qutab Minar station, named for the Qutb Minar."
    caveats: In on-screen captions, use 'Qutab Minar' for the station and 'Qutb Minar' for the monument.
- fact_136 [src_236, src_192]: Udyog Bhawan station was renamed Seva Teerth on 14 Feb 2026. DMRC's live station list now reads 'Seva Teerth (earlier Udyog Bhawan)'. Any map or caption saying 'Udyog Bhawan' is out of date.
    narration_line: "Seva Teerth (formerly Udyog Bhawan)."
    caveats: The Statesman report names a living political leader; do not name or show anyone in the film.
- fact_137 [src_237, src_238]: The southern terminus opened in 2010 as HUDA City Centre and was renamed Millennium City Centre Gurugram on 3 Jul 2023, after being renamed three times that day.
    narration_line: "All the way to Millennium City Centre in Gurugram."
    caveats: Use the current name in captions.
- fact_138 [src_219, src_239]: DMRC calls Hauz Khas (Yellow/Magenta interchange, 7 technical levels) its deepest station; the depth (about 29 m) is on the Magenta Line platforms, while the Yellow Line platforms are about 17 m deep.
    narration_line: "At Hauz Khas, my newer Magenta Line runs nearly thirty metres down, among the deepest stations under my streets."
    caveats: This is DMRC's own wording and the depth figure is not given. Newer Phase IV stations may be deeper. If used, attribute it: 'DMRC calls it its deepest station'.
- fact_139 [src_224, src_240]: Station coordinates: DMRC's published coordinates match OpenStreetMap to within 100 m for 30 of the 37 stations. Four DMRC coordinates appear wrong by 0.2 to 0.85 km, where OpenStreetMap and Wikidata agree with each other: Rohini Sector 18, 19 (845 m), Jahangirpuri (557 m), Adarsh Nagar (420 m; DMRC's point is the Indian Railways station) and Green Park (199 m). For those four, structured_data uses the OSM/Wikidata coordinates. New Delhi (290 m), Seva Teerth (170 m) and Vidhan Sabha (165 m) differ moderately; DMRC's values are kept for those (Wikidata agrees with DMRC for Seva Teerth and Vidhan Sabha).
    caveats: Coordinates are point markers for station buildings, good to about 100 m. Do not use them for precise walking-distance claims.
#### asiad-1982
- fact_140 [src_241]: The IX Asian Games were held in Delhi from 19 November to 4 December 1982. They were the first Asian Games run by the Olympic Council of Asia. Delhi was hosting for the second time, after the first Asian Games in 1951.
    narration_line: "In the winter of 1982, from the nineteenth of November to the fourth of December, I hosted the Asian Games for the second time."
    caveats: One Wikipedia medal-table page gives 12 November as the start date. The OCA page, the official source, says 19 November.

- fact_149 [src_262, src_267, src_268]: In People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (judgment of 18 Sep 1982, Justices P.N. [src_034] Wikipedia: Jantar Mantar, New Delhi
  The Jantar Mantar in New Delhi is an observatory, designed to be used with the naked eye. It is one of five Jantar Mantars in India. "Jantar Mantar" means 'instruments for measuring the harmony of the heavens'. It consists of 13 architectural astronomical instruments. The site is one of five built by Sawai Jai Singh of Jaipur, from 1723 onwards, revising the calendar and astronomical tables. Jai Singh, born in 1688 into a royal Rajput family that ruled the regional kingdom, was born into an era of education that maintained a keen interest in astronomy. There is a plaque fixed on one of the structures in the Jantar Mantar observatory in New Delhi that was placed there in 1910 mistakenly dating the construction of the complex to the year 1710. Later research, though, suggests 1724 as the actual year of construction. It is 723 feet (220 m) above sea level. The primary purpose of the observatory was to compile astronomical tables, and to predict the times and movements of the Sun, Moon and planets. Some of these purposes nowadays would be classified as astronomy. Completed in 1724, the Delhi Jantar Mantar had decayed considerably by the time of the 1857 uprising. The Ram Yantra, the Samrat Yantra, the Jai Prakash Yantra and the Misra Yantra are the distinct instruments of Jantar Mantar. The most famous of these structures, the Jaipur, had also deteriorated by the end of the nineteenth century until in 1901 when Maharaja Ram Singh set out to restore the instrument.

[src_089] Wikipedia: Khirki Mosque
  The Khirki Mosque (Arabic: مسجد خيركي; Hindi: खिड़की मस्जिद, दिल्ली) is a former mosque, now in partial ruins, located in Khirki Village, near Satpula, in South Delhi, India. The mosque was built by Khan-i-Jahan Junan Shah, the prime minister of Feroz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) of the Tughlaq Dynasty. The former mosque can be approached from Satpula or the seven–arched bridge on the edge of southern wall of Jahanpanah. The former mosque is a Monument of National Importance, administered by the Archaeological Survey of India. While construction within hundred metres of monuments designated as such are explicitly outlawed by the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, the mosque remains completely circumscribed by contemporaneous urban sprawl.

[src_001] Wikipedia: Chandni Chowk
  Chandni Chowk (meaning "Moonlight Square") is a street market square located in Old Delhi, India. One of the oldest and busiest markets in Delhi, the Mughal-era Red Fort straddles the eastern fringes of Chandni Chowk. It was built in 1650 by the Mughal Emperor, Shah Jahan, and designed by his daughter, Jahanara. The street spanning the market was historically divided by canals, engineered to reflect moonlight. These canals have since been closed and destroyed following British occupation, leaving behind a transformed urban landscape predisposed to congestion and chaos. It remains one of India's largest wholesale markets.
[src_002] Wikipedia: Red Fort
  The Red Fort (Lal Qila in Hindi; Hindi pronunciation: [laːl 'qɪlaː]) is a historic Mughal fort located in the Old Delhi area of Delhi, India. Serving as the main residence of the Mughal emperors, it was commissioned by Emperor Shah Jahan on the 12th of May 1639; the fort was constructed following his decision to shift the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi. Originally adorned in red and white, the fort's design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the architect of the Taj Mahal. The Red Fort is a prominent example of Mughal architecture from Shah Jahan's reign, combining Persian and Indian architectural styles. During the invasion by Nadir Shah of the Afsharid Empire in 1739, the fort was plundered and stripped of its artwork and jewels. Following the Indian Rebellion of 1857, many of its marble structures were demolished by the British, although the defensive walls remained largely intact. The fort was later repurposed as a military garrison. On 15 August 1947, the first Prime Minister of India, Jawaharlal Nehru, hoisted the Indian flag above the Lahori Gate, the main entrance of the Red Fort. Since then, the Prime Minister of India has ceremonially raised the national tricolour at the main gate each year on Independence Day, then delivering a nationally broadcast address from its ramparts. The Red Fort, as part of the Red Fort Complex, was recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.

[src_004] Wikipedia: Shahjahanabad
  Old Delhi (Hindustani: Purani Dilli), (historically Shahjahanabad), is a place in the Central Delhi district of Delhi, India. It was founded as a Walled City and officially named Shahjahanabad in 1648, upon Shah Jahan's decision to shift the imperial Mughal capital from Agra. The construction of the fortified city was completed in 1648, and it remained the capital of Mughal India until its fall in 1857, when the British Empire (whose Indian capital was at Calcutta) took over as paramount power in the Indian subcontinent. After the inauguration of New Delhi as the capital of India, the locality started to be colloquially known as Old Delhi in order to distinguish it from the capital city, or the rest of the NCT Region or National Capital Region. Old Delhi, or Shahjahanabad, rose as the capital of the Mughals for most of the empire's history, right from the rise and decline and demise of the empire. The major landmark monuments built during the Mughal era are the Red Fort, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Jama Masjid, and the Sri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir. After the start of British colonialism, the St. James' Church and the Lawrence Institute of Educational and Cultural Affairs, later known as Delhi Town Hall were built in the 19th century. … Only a few havelis are left and maintained.

[src_006] Wikipedia: Salimgarh Fort
  [personal memory removed at the maker's request] The fort was constructed during a period when the Mughal Empire had been temporarily overthrown; in 1540 CE, Sher Shah Suri had defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun and established the rule of the Sur Empire rule in Delhi. The Surid dynasty continued until 1555 CE, when Humayun regained control by defeating Sikandar Suri, the last ruler of the dynasty. During the Mughal period, particularly in later years, Salimgarh Fort continued to be of strategic significance. While constructing the Red Fort and the city of Shahjahanbad, several Mughal rulers, including Emperor Shah Jahan—who completed Shahjahanabad in 1639 CE—are believed to have camped at the fort. It is also said that Humayun camped there for three days before launching his successful campaign to recapture Delhi. The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb later converted the fort into a prison, a practice that was continued by the British after they took control of the fort in 1857. Salimgarh Fort is now part of the Red Fort Complex. The complex was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, obligating the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to undertake well-planned conservation measures for its preservation.

[src_008] Wikipedia: Kashmiri Gate, Delhi
  Kashmiri Gate, also spelled Kashmere/Cashmere Gate, is a historic gate located in Old Delhi, Delhi, India. It served as the northern entrance to the walled city of Shahjahanabad, the capital of the Mughal Empire. Built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in the mid-17th century, the gate is named after its proximity to the road that led to Kashmir. It holds historical significance not only for its architectural grandeur but also for its role in key events, including the 1857 Indian Rebellion. Today, Kashmiri Gate is a prominent landmark in Delhi, connecting several major roads and serving as a hub for the city's transportation network. Kashmiri Gate lends its name to the surrounding locality in North Delhi, situated in the Old Delhi area. It also serves as a significant road junction since it lies in close proximity to important landmarks such as the Red Fort, the Inter-State Bus Terminal (ISBT), and the Delhi Junction railway station.

[src_010] Wikipedia: Jama Masjid, Delhi
  The Masjid-i-Jehan-Numa, commonly known as the Jama Masjid, in Old Delhi area of Delhi, is one of the largest mosques in India. Its builder was the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, between 1644 and 1656, and it was inaugurated by its first Imam, Syed Abdul Ghafoor Shah Bukhari. Situated in the Mughal capital of Shahjahanabad (today Old Delhi), it served as the imperial mosque of the Mughal emperors until the demise of the empire in 1857. The Jama Masjid was regarded as a symbolic gesture of Mughal power across India. It was also a site of political significance during several key periods of British rule. It remains in active use, and is one of Delhi's most iconic sites, closely identified with the methods of Old Delhi. The mosque structure is a Monument of National Importance.

[src_014] Wikipedia: Ghalib ki Haveli
  Ghalib ki Haveli (ALA-LC: G̱ẖālib kī Ḥawelī IPA: [ˈɣɑːlɪb kiː ɦəˈʋeːliː], lit. 'Ghalib's Mansion') is a haveli in Gali Qasim Jan (lit. Its Mughal architecture reflects the period when the Mughal era was on the decline in India. The house was given to him by Hakim, a physician who is believed was an enthusiast of his poetry. [src_036] Wikipedia: Sacred Heart Cathedral, New Delhi

[src_038] Wikipedia: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib
  Gurdwara Bangla Sahib is one of the most prominent Sikh gurdwaras, or Sikh house of worship, in Delhi, India, and known for its association with the eighth Sikh Guru, Guru Har Krishan, as well as the holy pond inside its complex, known as the "Sarovar." Originally a bungalow of Raja Jai Singh I of Amber, it was rebuilt as a small shrine by Sikh General Sardar Baghel Singh in 1783. In the same year, there was reconstruction of nine Sikh shrines in Delhi. It is located near Connaught Place, New Delhi on Baba Kharak Singh Marg and it is recognisable by its golden dome and tall flagpole.
[src_040] Wikipedia: Laxminarayan Temple
  Laxminarayan Temple, commonly known as Birla Mandir, is a Hindu temple in New Delhi, India. Dedicated to Lakshmi and Vishnu in the dual representation of Lakshmi Narayana, it was built by the industrialist Jugal Kishore Birla between 1933 and 1939 and inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi agreed to inaugurate the temple on the condition that it would be open to people of all castes. The temple is built in the Orissan architectural style and was the first large Hindu temple built in Delhi in the 20th century colonial era. The temple complex covers about 3 hectares (7.5 acres) and includes shrines dedicated to Shiva, Ganesha, Hanuman and Buddha, as well as fountains, gardens and a Geeta Bhawan, a hall used for religious discourses. It is one of Delhi's major Hindu temples and attracts large numbers of devotees during Janmashtami and Diwali.

[src_042] Wikipedia: Secretariat Building, New Delhi
  The Secretariat Building or Central Secretariat housed the most important offices and ministries of the Government of India, including the Cabinet Secretariat, at Raisina Hill, New Delhi. The Secretariat buildings are two blocks of symmetrical buildings, North Block and South Block, on opposite sides of the great axis of Rajpath, and flanking the Rashtrapati Bhavan (President's House). The buildings were designed by Herbert Baker and form a part of Lutyens' layout for New Delhi. As part of the Central Vista Redevelopment Project, the Government of India commissioned the nearby Seva Teerth (Executive Enclave) and the Kartavya Bhavan (Common Central Secretariat) to modernize and consolidate central government offices with phased moves from the Secretariat Building occurring in 2025–2026. The North Block and South Block buildings are currently being repurposed as the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum. Seva Teerth is an integrated administrative complex housing the new Prime Minister's Office (PMO), the Cabinet Secretariat, and the National Security Council Secretariat and the Kartavya Bhavan houses key ministries and departments that previously occupied the Secretariat Building and various older ministerial and government buildings across New Delhi.
[src_043] Wikipedia: Rashtrapati Bhavan
  The Rashtrapati Bhavan (ISO: Rāṣṭrapati Bhavana; lit. 'President's House'), formerly Viceroy's House (1931–1947) and Government House (1947–1950) is the official residence of the President of India, located at the western end of Rajpath, Raisina Hill in New Delhi. The building was designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker in Delhi Order based on Indo-Saracenic architecture. The construction began in 1912 and the building was completed in 1929. The building, initially known as Viceroy's House, housed the Viceroy of India from 1931 until India's independence. After Independence, it briefly served as the Government House, housing the Governor General of India from 1947 to 1950. … The main building is spread across four floors and a basement, consisting of 340 rooms and featuring a total of 2.50-kilometre-long corridors, spread across a floor area of 200,000 square metres (2,200,000 sq ft), including the President's official residence, reception halls, guest rooms and offices. It is situated in a 320 acres (130 hectares) presidential estate that includes gardens, open spaces, residences for security and staff, stables, offices and other utilities. With over 200,000 square metres (2,200,000 sq ft) of total usable floor area of the H-shaped main building, the Rashtrapati Bhavan is the largest official residence by total floor area of any head of state in the world, followed by, the Istana Nurul Iman in Brunei and the Quirinal Palace in Italy.

[src_045] Wikipedia: India Gate
  The India Gate (formerly known as All India War Memorial) is a war memorial arch that’s located near the Rajpath (officially called Kartavya Path) on the eastern edge of the "ceremonial axis" of New Delhi, India. It stands as a memorial to exactly 74,187 Indian soldiers of the British Indian Army who died between 1914 and 1921 during the First World War, in places like France, Flanders, Mesopotamia, Persia, East Africa, Gallipoli, in the Near and Far East, and the 1919 Third Anglo-Afghan War. Around 13,300 British servicemen's names, including some soldiers and officers from the United Kingdom, are also inscribed onto the gate. Designed by architect sir Edwin Lutyens, the gate evokes the architectural style of the ancient Roman triumphal arches, such as the Arch of Constantine in Rome, Italy and later memorial arches; it is often compared to the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, France and the Gateway of India in Mumbai, India. Following the Indo-Pakistani war of 1971, a structure consisting of a black marble plinth with a reversed rifle, capped by a war helmet and bounded by four eternal flames, was built beneath the archway. This structure, called Amar Jawan Jyoti (Flame of the Immortal Soldier), had between 1971 and 2019, until replaced by the Indian national war memorial, served as India's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. … India Gate is often a location for civil society protests, and is popular among tourists.

[src_047] Wikipedia: Old Parliament House, New Delhi
  The Old Parliament House, officially known as the Samvidhan Sadan (Constitution House) and formerly known as the Council House, was the seat of the Parliament of India between 26 January 1950 and 18 September 2023. It housed the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha (the lower and upper houses) respectively in India's bicameral parliament for nearly 73 years. Earlier it had served as the seat of the Imperial Legislative Council between 18 January 1927 and 15 August 1947, and the Constituent Assembly of India between 15 August 1947 and 26 January 1950. The building was designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker and was constructed between 1921 and 1927. It was opened in January 1927 as the seat of the Imperial Legislative Council. Following the Indian Independence in 1947, it was taken over by the Constituent Assembly of India, and then became the seat of the Indian Parliament on 26 January 1950 with India becoming a republic following the adoption of the Indian Constitution. A new Parliament House built adjacent to this building was inaugurated on 28 May 2023, replacing the old Parliament building.

[src_088] Wikipedia: Malviya Nagar (Delhi)
  Malviya Nagar is a residential locality in South Delhi. Situated between Saket and Hauz Khas, its namesake is the freedom fighter Madan Mohan Malviya. Malviya Nagar was initially a part of the Shahpur Jat village, in which after partition was populated in the 1950s by refugees from Pakistan, after the Partition of India. A large portion of the population were ethnic Rajasthani, U.P., Haryanvi, Punjabis and Sindhis, as well as Afghan refugees who were displaced during the Soviet–Afghan War in the 1970s and 1980s. Today, Malviya Nagar is bounded by Panchsheel Enclave in the north, Sheikh Sarai in the east, Saket in the south and Hauz Khas in the west. Sub localities that are part of Malviya Nagar include Geetanjali Enclave, Navjeevan Vihar, Bhavishya Nidhi Enclave, Shivalik colony, Begumpur, Sarvodaya Enclave and MMTC Colony. It is serviced by the Malviya Nagar station located on the Yellow Line of the Delhi Metro. Malviya Nagar is also home to Delhi Police's Training School. in 2026, A fire broke out which kills 21 people.
[src_094] Wikipedia: Qutb Minar
  The Qutb Minar, also spelled Qutub Minar and Qutab Minar, is a minaret and victory tower, built during the Delhi sultanate, and comprising the Qutb complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Mehrauli, South Delhi, India. It was mostly built between 1199 and 1220, contains 399 steps, and is one of the most frequented heritage spots in the city. After defeating Prithviraj Chauhan, the last Hindu ruler of Delhi before the Ghurid conquest of the region, Qutab-ud-din Aibak initiated the construction of the victory tower, but only managed to finish the first level. It was to mark the beginning of Islamic rule in the region. Successive dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate continued the construction, and, in 1368, Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top parts and added a cupola. It can be compared to the 62-metre all-brick Minaret of Jam in Afghanistan, of c. 1190, which was constructed a decade or so before the probable start of the Delhi tower. The surfaces of both are elaborately decorated with inscriptions and geometric patterns. The Qutb Minar has a shaft that is fluted with "superb stalactite bracketing under the balconies" at the top of each stage. In general, minarets were slow to be used in India and are often detached from the main mosque where they exist.

[src_096] Wikipedia: Iron pillar of Delhi
  The iron pillar of Delhi is a metal structure 7.21 metres (23 feet 8 inches) high with a 41-centimetre (16 in) diameter that was constructed by Chandragupta II (reigned c. 375–415 CE), and now stands in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli in Delhi, India. The metals used in its construction have a rust-resistant composition. The pillar weighs more than six tonnes and is thought to have been erected elsewhere, possibly outside the Udayagiri Caves, and moved to its present location by Anangpal Tomar in the 11th century.

[src_098] Wikipedia: Qutb Minar complex
  The Qutb Minar complex are monuments and buildings from the Delhi Sultanate at Mehrauli in Delhi, India. Construction of the Qutub Minar "victory tower" in the complex, named after the religious figure Sufi Saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, was begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who later became the first Sultan of Delhi of the Mamluk dynasty (Gulam Vansh). It was continued by his successor Iltutmish (a.k.a. Altamash), and finally completed much later by Firoz Shah Tughlaq, a Sultan of Delhi from the Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1412) in 1368 AD. The Qubbat-ul-Islam Mosque (Dome of Islam), later corrupted into Quwwat-ul Islam, stands next to the Qutb Minar. The Qutub Minar also bears numerous inscriptions in Arabic and Nagari characters at various locations, which reveal its history. Many subsequent rulers, including the Tughlaqs, Alauddin Khalji and the British added structures to the complex. Apart from the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat ul-Islam Mosque, other structures in the complex include the Alai Darwaza gate, the Alai Minar and the Iron pillar. Inside the complex lie the tombs of Iltutmish, Alauddin Khalji and Imam Zamin. Today, the adjoining area spread over with a host of old monuments, including Balban's tomb, has been developed by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) as the Mehrauli Archaeological Park, and INTACH has restored some 40 monuments in the Park.

response.title: One Ticket, 800 Years
response.logline: One Yellow Line ride from Chandni Chowk to Qutab Minar carries Delhi forward from Shah Jahan's city of 1639 to 1931 and 1947, then turns the clock back through the Tughlaq and Tomar ruins to the Qutb of around 1199 and an iron pillar older than any of them - a city that keeps being rebuilt by people who arrive.
response.music_prompt: Instrumental only, no vocals and no singing: a soft tanpura drone opens the film as a warm invitation, joined by sarangi and light finger cymbals; a bansuri flute enters with the map ride and a slow, unhurried tabla pulse at about 72 bpm carries the journey, brightening slightly as the years leap from 1639 to 1931 and 1947, then thinning to sparse strings, drone and a single flute at the Qutb Minar and the iron pillar, before softening again for the personal story and the closing line; a brief, gentle swell sits under each year card, and the piece ends on a warm resolved chord that sustains under the last words, total length about 160 seconds.

claims.text: The film promises eight hundred years of the city on a single ticket, as the maker's own framing of the title.
Shah Jahan founded Shahjahanabad, today's Old Delhi, in 1639.
The Red Fort is part of Shah Jahan's walled capital at the edge of Chandni Chowk.
Jahanara Begum, Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, laid out Chandni Chowk with a sarai and gardens.
A canal ran down the middle of Chandni Chowk and an octagonal pool reflected the moonlight.
Tradition gives Chandni Chowk its name from the moonlight reflected in that pool.
Shah Jahan's Jama Masjid was completed in 1656.
About five thousand workers built the Jama Masjid.
Jantar Mantar, at Patel Chowk, was completed in 1724.
Jantar Mantar is an observatory of huge stone instruments for measuring the heavens.
New Delhi was formally inaugurated as the capital on 13 February 1931 by the Viceroy.
Up to 23,000 labourers worked on the Viceroy's House at the peak of construction.
The Viceroy's House is now Rashtrapati Bhavan.
About half a million refugees entered Delhi after Partition.
About 330,000 of Delhi's Muslims left after Partition, so people moved in both directions.
Malviya Nagar was one of the new colonies laid out after Partition for refugees.
The new colonies were planned with their own markets, schools, temples and gurdwaras.
From Chandni Chowk to Saket the Yellow Line runs underground, and the train comes up into daylight only as it nears Qutab Minar.
The Qutb Minar was begun around 1199 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak.
Iltutmish completed the Qutb Minar.
Iltutmish made Delhi the capital of the sultanate.
The iron pillar in the Qutb complex dates from the 5th century.
The pillar's iron is rich in phosphorus, which forms a protective layer that greatly slows corrosion.
The pillar is more than 1,600 years old and has barely rusted.
